newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas free trade meeting not seen reaching deal.
newsitem.headline: Americas free trade meeting not seen reaching deal.

text.p: Ministers from 34 nations meet on Friday for preliminary talks on how to establish free trade throughout the western hemisphere, but they were not expected to reach agreement.
"It is impossible that an agreement will arise here," the secretary general of the Organisation of American States Cesar Gaviria, attending the talks as an observer, told reporters on Thursday.

Ministers from all the region's countries except Cuba began arriving in Brazil's third-largest city for a meeting on Friday that will set the groundwork for the next presidential summit of the Americas in Santiago, Chile, next year.
The ministers are expected to announce that formal negotiation of the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) will begin after the Santiago summit in March 1998.

The FTAA plan was born at the previous hemispheric summit in Miami in 1994 and envisages knocking down tariffs from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, creating a free trade area of nearly one billion consumers.
But disagreement exists between the United States and South America's Mercosur trade bloc, which groups Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, on how fast to proceed.
The United States wants everything from tariff reductions to subsidies to be discussed at the same time.
Mercosur, and in particular Brazil which faces a widening trade deficit, wants to split the talks into stages, with tariff cuts left until last.

Jorge Campbell, Argentina's secretary of international relations and Buenos Aires' chief FTAA negotiator, said the two sides were stuck on whether to say they "will" or they "should" start formal talks after the Santiago summit.

He said there was continuing disagreement on whether FTAA signatory countries needed to arrive at Santiago with a consensus on the nature of the negotiations or whether they could leave that difficult task for later.
In addition, Campbell said the ministers would have to reach agreement on Friday on whether to allow the labour movement more involvement in the negotiation process.
Brazilian officials insisted they had made great advances in deputy minister-level talks that began on Tuesday and were supposed to draft a declaration for Friday's meeting.
Parallel to the official trade talks, more than 2,000 businessmen from across the Americas were debating the FTAA.
U.S. officials, keeping a low profile until the arrival on Thursday of U.S. Trade Representive Charlene Barschefsky, Washington's chief negotiator, were not available to comment.
Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso was due to address the businessmen's forum on Thursday before opening the ministerial meeting in the evening.
